title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab
talk_summary: Amazon AGI Lab demos two open-sourced 'perception agent' primitives: a deterministic Chrome extension that turns point/click/draw annotations on a live web page into a JSON change spec plus an AI-friendly prompt, and a 'visual verification' skill that crawls the site, generates Gherkin user flows, replays them in a browser, and emits a pass/fail report. They wire these into a coding agent via an 'agent bridge' so annotate → apply changes → verify runs as one loop, with a human only reviewing the final report.

takeaways.technique: Visual verification as a gated, replayable check with auto-generated Gherkin flows
takeaways.what_they_do: A skill crawls the site once to discover links/content, generates Gherkin user-flow specs, then on each run drives a real browser through those flows against design artifacts and produces a report.

takeaways.technique: Deterministic annotation → JSON spec → agent prompt (no inference in the capture step)
takeaways.what_they_do: The Chrome extension is pure client-side: user points/clicks/draws and describes changes, exports a JSON file plus a prompt that a coding agent consumes; no model is involved in producing the spec.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this has nothing to do with inference. This is purely deterministic. It just outputs JSON, doesn't have It's not tied to any model

takeaways.technique: Agent bridge: one button closes annotate → apply → verify loop
takeaways.what_they_do: A small local bridge service receives the extension's 'apply changes' request, forwards the prompt to the coding agent CLI, then triggers the verification skill and surfaces a report link — human only checks the report.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have built uh something called agent bridge that will automatically uh take the annotations and up- give prompted to the coding agent

takeaways.technique: Verification report as the human review artifact
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of a human watching the agent work, the loop ends with a generated report (with model reasoning/logs) that the human reviews after a break.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you basically apply the changes and go grab a lunch or like break and then come back and just see uh the verification report

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue partial reliability destroys the gains because you must debug every run, and so invest in simulated environments/RL to raise success rates rather than adding more features.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If my agent works 50% of the time, it doesn't work at all.

takeaways.technique: Package verification as an installable skill for coding agents
takeaways.what_they_do: They ship the verification capability as a skill installable on Claude Code/Kiro (and an MCP server), so any coding agent can invoke it without bespoke integration.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when I say skill, it is actually a skill that you can install on Claude or Keynote
